query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, the stability of the phase distribution and the attainment of desirable mechanical and environmental properties are controlled by the formation of finely dispersed, coherent nanoscale precipitates during controlled aging. These precipitates (e.g., γ′-type) reduce lattice strain and block dislocation and defect motion, thereby simultaneously improving high‐temperature strength, radiation tolerance, environmental resistance, and cryogenic toughness. However, if the aging is extended beyond an optimum period, precipitate coarsening will lead to phase instability and a deterioration of toughness and environmental performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy in a solution-annealed, disordered matrix state with negligible precipitate formation.
generation.intervention: Application of a controlled aging heat treatment at approximately 750 °C for variable time durations (optimal aging vs. over-aging).
generation.conditions: Heat treatment in a controlled atmosphere at 750 °C with well-defined aging times, while keeping alloy composition (and minor alloying additions) constant.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale, coherent precipitates (e.g., γ′-phase or related intermetallics) that form within the matrix.
generation.mechanism: The controlled heat treatment promotes the nucleation and growth of coherent precipitates that relieve lattice strains and obstruct the motion of dislocations and radiation-induced defects. This precipitate formation enhances high-temperature yield strength, mitigates radiation damage, and supports environmental and cryogenic performance. Excessive aging, however, leads to precipitate coarsening, loss of coherency, and impaired toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under an optimized aging schedule, one should observe a uniform distribution of nanoscale precipitates, correlating with increased yield strength and balanced toughness (including cryogenic performance) and improved radiation and environmental resistance compared to the solution-annealed baseline. In contrast, over-aged samples will show coarsened precipitates and a deterioration of these properties.
generation.baseline: The solution-annealed state with a disordered matrix and minimal precipitate impact, where standard mechanical and environmental properties are observed.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys processed under similar conditions; deviations in composition, significantly different processing temperatures, or the introduction of different alloying elements might lead to alternative phase behaviors that fall outside this framework.
generation.uncertainty: While the general mechanism linking nanoscale precipitate formation to multi-property enhancement is supported by existing studies, the precise aging times, optimal precipitate sizes, and volume fractions that yield the ideal balance among high-temperature strength, radiation tolerance, environmental resistance, and cryogenic toughness remain to be quantified. The sensitivity of the mechanism to minor compositional variations also requires further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of identically composed Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni samples. Divide the set into a control batch (solution-annealed, without aging) and several test batches aged at 750 °C for varying durations (e.g., short, optimal, and extended aging periods). Characterize the microstructures using transmission electron microscopy and atom probe tomography to quantify precipitate size, distribution, and volume fraction. Measure mechanical properties (yield strength, toughness at cryogenic temperatures) and simulate radiation tolerance (via irradiation tests or defect density measurements).
measurements: Nanoscale precipitate size distribution and volume fraction
Yield strength via standard mechanical testing
Radiation-induced defect density or resistance measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If aging at 750 °C does not produce a significant, time-dependent formation of coherent nanoscale precipitates, or if the observed mechanical and environmental properties do not correlate with the precipitate characteristics (i.e., optimal properties are not linked to an optimal precipitate regime versus the solution-annealed state), then the hypothesis that precipitate-mediated stabilization governs phase behavior and property retention is falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractThe efficient energy use in multiple sectors of modern industry is partly based on the efficient use of high-strength, high-performance alloys that retain remarkable mechanical properties at elevated and high temperatures. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) represent the most recent class of these materials with a high potential for high-temperature high-strength applications. Aside from their chemical composition and microstructure-property relationship, limited information on the effect of heat treatment as a decisive factor for alloy design is available in the literature. This work intends to contribute to this research topic by investigating the effect of heat treatment on the microstructure and mechanical performance of an Al4.4Co26Cr19Fe18Ni27Ti5.6 HEA. The solution annealed state is compared to aged states obtained at different heat treatment times at 750 °C. AbstractIn order to explore the effect of alloying on the microstructures and mechanical properties of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), 0.1, 0.2, and 0.3 at.% V, Mo, and B were added to the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy in this work. The effects of the elements and contents on the phase composition, microstructures, mechanical properties, and fracture mechanism were investigated. The results showed that the crystal structures of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEAs remained unchanged, and the alloys were still composed of FCC and BCC structures, whose content varied with the addition of alloying elements. After alloying, the aggregation of Co, Cr, Al, and Ni elements remained unchanged, and the V and Mo were distributed in both dendritic and interdendritic phases. The tensile strengths of the alloys all exceeded 1000 MPa when the V and Mo elements were added, and the Mo0.2 alloy had the highest tensile strength, of 1346.3 MPa, and fracture elongation, of 24.6%. The alloys with the addition of V and Mo elements showed a mixed ductile and brittle fracture, while the B-containing alloy presented a cleavage fracture.
